newsitem.title: GERMANY: EMU choice should take account of tax issue - Gaddum.
newsitem.headline: EMU choice should take account of tax issue - Gaddum.

text.p: European tax policies should play a role in the decision as to which states are eligible to join the region's planned single currency in 1999, Bundesbank council member Johann Wilhelm Gaddum said on Tuesday.

In an interview with the Wall Street Journal Europe, Gaddum said tax harmonisation in Europe "still leaves a lot to be desired" and was "one of the points that should be taken into consideration when one talks about the possibility of monetary union."
Gaddum said tax harmonisation played an important role in judging how a unified market developed.

"The (Maastricht) treaty has five convergence criteria, but it also asks how the unified market has developed. One can well ask whether the unified market has been distorted through differing tax systems," he said.
Gaddum said further harmonisation "doesn't mean the weakening of tax sovereignty, but it means a particular agreement on equality in the principles of taxation."
He was not specific on the timing of such an agreement.

Germany is traditionally critical of differing tax regimes in its neighbouring countries, especially Austria and Luxembourg, the beneficiaries of billions of marks in flight capital after Germany introduced an investment income tax.

Gaddum also said that the European Commission's proposals for a stability pact, a system to impose sanctions on countries failing to keep their finances in order after the Euro launch, "does not correspond entirely with (the Bundesbank's) views.
He said he felt government officials in Bonn were "holding back from what we think is important" on some points in this issue.

Gaddum also urged more action on German financial market reforms, saying Bonn should agree to convert existing debt into the Euro as soon as the new currency is introduced. He also said he hoped Bonn would allow the practice of "stripping" long term bonds -- removing coupons for separate sale. --Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525
